stories.title: Elastic shows how to join Claude activity with application traces
stories.summary: Elastic documents two export paths for Claude activity: platform records from the console and application records from the SDK.
body: Elastic, a platform for searching operational data, documents how to investigate Claude activity alongside application traces. Its October 27 guide uses OpenTelemetry, a standard for exporting telemetry. A span records one operation. Console export supplies platform activity; SDK export adds work inside the application.

For illustration, a slow assistant might spend time in a model request or in a custom tool. Sending both streams helps distinguish those steps. The guide says console export cannot see work that stays inside your process. That requires application instrumentation.

Setup needs a Claude organization administrator, an Elastic trace endpoint and a key allowed to write traces. The guide includes a test-span query to check delivery. Full-content mode includes conversation text; metadata-only mode omits it. Claude export is in public beta. Elastic’s GenAI tab is a technical preview on Serverless and Cloud Hosted 9.6; older versions show key values.
stories.takeaway: For teams exporting Claude traces: test both platform and application coverage, and choose content retention before enabling export.

stories.title: Langfuse records more facts about gateway model calls
stories.summary: Langfuse 4.71.0 expands gateway generation records and fixes model attribution for routed LiteLLM calls.
body: Langfuse is a platform for recording and evaluating AI application activity. Its 4.71.0 release adds model, key-owner, byte and upstream-error facts to generation records from its AI gateway, the component through which applications send model requests. These fields give operators more evidence about a call than a success or failure result alone.

For illustration, a team investigating a failed assistant request could examine the recorded upstream error and key owner while checking which model handled the call. That is a debugging use for the added facts, not a claim that the release automatically identifies the root cause. The release separately fixes OpenTelemetry recording to use the model dispatched by LiteLLM for routed calls, where the selected model can differ from the original request.

Other changes extract nested messages and Pydantic agent history into normalized input and output, and count self-hosted traces and observations from the events table in events-only mode. The notes describe implementation changes without a completeness benchmark. Teams should confirm their own records after upgrading, particularly when routing or ingestion settings differ between environments.
stories.takeaway: For gateway operators: compare a routed call’s recorded model and error fields with provider evidence after upgrading.

stories.title: Weir checks where planted credentials leave an agent
stories.summary: Weir’s developer describes deterministic credential-flow tests that distinguish a clean run from a required path that was never exercised.
body: Weir is a tool for checking whether credentials cross an AI agent’s boundaries. In its original Show HN announcement, the developer describes planting fake credentials where real ones would live, running the agent’s normal flows, and searching the resulting telemetry and outgoing requests for those exact values. The report identifies destinations without printing the credential.

For illustration, a fake API key placed in an agent’s environment might appear in a trace even though it was intended only for authentication. The test can expose that unwanted copy. If a required path was not exercised, the developer says Weir reports an incomplete result rather than a clean one. The test is deterministic and offline; Linux can additionally restrict outside network access.

A separate Claude Code mode observes known credentials entering a session or leaving in tool calls, with an optional tool-result redaction hook. These are limited checks: matching does not cover hashed, split or truncated credentials. Redaction cannot undo a credential already pasted into a conversation, and failed-command output can still reach the model. The announcement supplies the developer’s claims, not an independent security audit.
stories.takeaway: For agent developers: test credential destinations with fake values and investigate incomplete runs before accepting a clean verdict.

stories.title: Langfuse backports webhook-secret and access checks to version 3
stories.summary: The version 3 maintenance release masks and encrypts legacy webhook headers and requires secrets again when destinations change.
body: Langfuse records AI application activity and supports automation around that data. Its 3.225.15 maintenance release brings four fixes to the version 3 branch, including two affecting secrets used by outbound integrations. The release notes describe masking and encrypting legacy webhook headers, plus requiring secrets again when a webhook or PostHog destination changes.

For illustration, an operator changing the destination of an existing automation should review which credentials authorize the new connection. Requiring those secrets again makes the destination change an explicit configuration step. This is an illustrative administrative workflow; the release notes do not describe an observed exploit, affected customer count, or a complete migration procedure.

The same release checks that a project referenced by an invitation belongs to the organization and validates an annotation queue when items are added. Annotation queues organize examples for human review, so their access and item-handling checks matter to evaluation operations. All four entries are identified as backports. This maintenance update is distinct from the version 4 gateway telemetry changes; version 3 operators should review the linked fixes for their deployment.
stories.takeaway: For version 3 administrators: review automation destinations and secret handling when planning this maintenance update.
